Pilot report (P4): 2,000 GTDB R232 genomes

Date: 2026-11-06. Run: ./run.sh pilot, two Nextflow sessions (8 h 46 m launch, plus a 1 h 05 m resume that added the steps wired in after launch). Machine: 32 cores, 125 GB RAM. Detailed outputs:

  • QC report — yield per step
  • Aim 1 report — prediction
  • Aim 2 report — association
  • PICRUSt2 comparison — head-to-head, ordination, all outputs
  • Cost report — CPU and wall time per step

1. Engineering

check result
tasks failed 0 (100 in run 1, 89 new + 81 cached in the resume)
usable genomes 1,999 / 2,000 (99.95 %; 1 genome without a full-length 16S). Design target ≥ 90 %
in-silico PCR success V4 98.0 %, V3V4 95.9 % (archaea 90.7 % / 77.5 %)
disk db/ 51 GB (eggNOG 48 GB), work/pilot 9.5 GB, results/pilot 228 MB
peak memory PICRUSt2 61.5 GB; eggNOG 11.6 GB; ALIGN_16S 10.3 GB; AIM1_PREDICT 7.4 GB; others < 4 GB

Problems found and fixed during the pilot:

  • BUILD_TARGETS took 2.3 h on one core, all in give_completeness (~4.7 s per genome; ~70 h at 55k). Now runs on 16 genome chunks in parallel, output identical to serial (D067).
  • The resume re-ran ALIGN_16S and its dependants once, because deep caching was enabled after the pilot was launched (the hash mode changed). Not a bug: the test profile resumes with full caching. cost_report.py now counts each task once (D068).

2. Cost extrapolation

Per-genome steps cost 283 CPU-s per genome, 98 % of it eggNOG-mapper (runs one batch at a time on all cores, 26.5 cores busy on average).

step pilot (2k) 20k genomes 54,963 genomes
eggNOG (elapsed, serial batches) 5.8 h ~58 h ~160 h (6.7 days)
fetch + barrnap + genes (run alongside eggNOG) 2.4 CPU-h ~24 CPU-h ~66 CPU-h
BUILD_TARGETS (after D067) ~10 min ~1.5 h ~4 h
Aim 1 (15 arm × level tasks) 6.6 CPU-h ~70–150 CPU-h ~200–400 CPU-h
Aim 2 (pyseer LMM, as built) 8.8 CPU-h see §6 infeasible as built (see §6)
PICRUSt2 13 min, 61.5 GB needs chunking needs chunking
PICRUSt2 comparison 25 min ~4 h (linear, not measured) ~11 h (linear, not measured)
disk, work/ 9.5 GB ~95 GB ~260 GB

Aim 1 is extrapolated from its parts: the k-NN identity matrix (test × train, per fold) grows with n², and the forest grows with about n log n. At 55k the largest identity block is ~11k × 44k (2 GB float32), so it fits.

3. Aim 1 — can 16S predict function?

Yes. The signal is phylogenetic, and it fades with distance to the nearest reference.

  • Gain in per-genome KO-set F1 over the null model (training-set prevalence), random forest, full-length 16S: random split +0.23, genus holdout +0.20, family +0.16, order +0.12, class +0.07. All 95 % CIs exclude 0.
  • Median per-KO AUROC, full-length random forest: 0.91 (random) → 0.85 (family) → 0.70 (class).
  • Accuracy rises steadily with 16S identity to the nearest training genome (fig 1). KO F1 is ~0.60 below 85 % identity and ~0.90 at ≥ 99 %. Tree distance and 16S identity agree (Spearman −0.79).
  • Learned models do not beat 5-NN at this scale. RF and LightGBM are worse than 5-NN at the random, genus and family levels, by 0.01–0.03 in F1 and MAE. At order and class they are equal or slightly better: COG Bray-Curtis +0.004–0.008, KO F1 not significant. The 16S works as a phylogenetic placement. Individual positions do not add usable information beyond "who is my closest relative" — at least not with 2k genomes.
  • Amplicons cost 9–35 % of the gain. RF KO F1 gain is 0.226 / 0.210 / 0.206 (full / V3V4 / V4) at the random level, and 0.073 / 0.055 / 0.060 at class. V3V4 and V4 are indistinguishable.
  • PICRUSt2 ties with 5-NN when it is fair (§5). On the 1,205 genomes not in PICRUSt2's own reference, its KO F1 is 0.783; ours on the same genomes: 5-NN 0.785, 1-NN 0.774. On the 794 genomes in its reference it scores 0.94, which is leakage, not skill.
  • Note: the null model's median per-KO AUROC is below 0.5 (0.38–0.47). The null predicts one constant per fold; when a held-out clade carries a KO, the training prevalence is lower. Pooled over folds, that anti-correlates. The null's per-genome scores, used for "gain over null", are unaffected.

Accuracy against 16S similarity to the closest training genome. Each test genome is binned by the full-length 16S identity to its most similar training genome. Lines are models; the dashed grey line is the null, which ignores the 16S. Panels: KO set F1 (higher is better), module completeness error and COG profile dissimilarity (lower is better).

Takeaway: every model improves steadily as the closest reference gets closer, and the models stay close to each other. The 16S predicts function through its nearest relatives; learned models do not escape that dependence.

Gain over the null as test genomes become more distant. Left to right, whole genera, families, orders and classes are kept out of training. Points are mean gain over the null with 95 % CIs; above 0 means the 16S helps.

Takeaway: the gain shrinks with distance but stays above 0 for KOs and modules even for unseen classes. 1-NN (blue) drops fastest; averaging 5 neighbours or learning (forest, LightGBM) holds up better far from the reference.

Full-length 16S against the V4 and V3-V4 amplicons (random forest, gain over the null).

Takeaway: the amplicons keep most of the signal; they lose a roughly constant amount at every level, which is a larger share of the small gain at order and class. V4 and V3-V4 are nearly identical.

4. Aim 2 — 16S alleles associated with function beyond phylogeny

1,795 bacteria, 3,252 alleles (3,106 unique patterns), 4,616 phenotypes (4,233 KOs, 383 modules), pyseer LMM with GTDB-tree kinship.

  • Calibration is good. Median genomic inflation λ is 0.94 (KOs) and 0.99 (modules), with 10–90 % range 0.6–1.2.
  • The positive control works. Reverse gyrase (K03170, hyperthermophily) has 187 Bonferroni hits, including the top 12 overall. Its positively associated alleles are 74 % G/C, against 47 % background: the known GC–thermostability relation of rRNA stems, recovered without being told.
  • 11,591 Bonferroni hits (2,518 phenotypes, 2,272 alleles); 20,801 at BH-FDR < 0.05. 10.7 % of tests were flagged by pyseer and excluded.
  • The homoplasy filter does not discriminate. All 2,272 hit alleles change more than once on the tree (Fitch). At 1,795 genomes almost every allele is homoplasic, so "> 1 change" separates nothing. Many hits are likely still clade-tagging that the kinship term absorbs only partly. A stricter criterion is needed before reading individual hits as biology (§7, question 3).

Calibration of the association test. One λ per phenotype; λ = 1 means the phylogenetic correction removes the inflation caused by shared ancestry, above 1 means leftover structure (false positives), below 1 means conservative.

Takeaway: both distributions centre on 1 (65 % of KOs between 0.8 and 1.2), so the test is not inflated by ancestry. The KO tail below 0.5 means a conservative test for those KOs: less power, not false positives.

Where the significant alleles sit along the 16S (E. coli numbering; grey bands = variable regions V1-V9).

Takeaway: hits spread along the whole gene and are not enriched in variable regions (43 % of hits, against 48 % of tested alleles). The highest peaks sit near position 125 (conserved stretch between V1 and V2), at the end of V2 (~235) and in V5 (~830-860). Positions with very many hits mark clades rather than single functions, which is why the homoplasy criterion (§7, question 3) matters.

5. PICRUSt2 head-to-head

Full report: PICRUSt2 comparison. Fair test set: the 1,205 genomes not in PICRUSt2's reference (same GTDB accession = in; 794 are). Our predictions are out-of-fold (full-length 16S, random split), so no genome is ever predicted from itself.

Q1. Does our approach beat PICRUSt2? Overall, no: it ties.

per genome, mean (unseen genomes) PICRUSt2 ours, best ours − PICRUSt2 (95 % CI) genomes where ours is better
KO F1 0.783 0.785 (5-NN) +0.003 (−0.006 to +0.011) 39 %
module completeness error 0.077 0.079 (1-NN) +0.002 worse (−0.002 to +0.006) 36 %

The random forest is worse overall (KO F1 −0.024), but it is more precise: 0.836 against 0.797. It calls fewer KOs, and more of them are right. The tie comes with a handicap for us: each fold learns from ~1,600 genomes; PICRUSt2's reference has 27,870. At full scale ours learn from ~44,000.

Q2. Is our approach better anywhere? Yes, in three places.

  1. Novel genomes. In the most novel fifth (NSTI > 0.36), KO F1 is 0.71 (5-NN) against 0.60 (PICRUSt2), and module error 0.086 (1-NN) against 0.128. PICRUSt2 wins clearly for genomes close to its reference (NSTI < 0.03: F1 0.91 vs 0.85; module error 0.039 vs 0.067). The lines cross in the middle quintile, NSTI 0.08–0.16 (figure below).
  2. Clades poorly covered by PICRUSt2. Archaea: 0.745 vs 0.639. Patescibacteriota (CPR): 0.637 vs 0.350. PICRUSt2 is better in every well-sampled bacterial phylum (Pseudomonadota 0.877 vs 0.811, Actinomycetota, Bacteroidota, Bacillota, Acidobacteriota, Chloroflexota).
  3. Ranking genomes per KO, and the shape of the functional landscape. Per-KO AUROC: random forest higher on 99 % of 4,405 KOs (median 0.90 vs 0.81). PICRUSt2's copy numbers are coarse (0, 1, 2), so it ranks genomes poorly, worst for core genes carried by ~90 % of genomes. Between-genome functional distances correlate with the truth at Mantel r 0.94 (1-NN) against 0.72 (PICRUSt2) for KOs, and 0.88 against 0.54 for modules (Q4).

Where PICRUSt2 is better: per-KO F1 of the presence calls (better on 66 % of KOs against 5-NN), and anything close to its reference.

Accuracy by novelty, unseen genomes. Left and right: genomes binned by PICRUSt2's NSTI (tree distance to its nearest reference genome; quintiles). Middle: binned by 16S identity to our nearest training genome. Each point is one method's mean per-genome score in that bin; pink = PICRUSt2.

Takeaway: PICRUSt2 is the better tool for genomes close to its reference. It loses accuracy faster with novelty, and in the most novel fifth our models are ahead on both KOs and modules.

Q3. Where is the output? Small tables, figures and the report: reports/pilot/picrust2_comparison/. Everything, including the large call tables: results/pilot/picrust2_comparison/:

  • per_genome.tsv: one row per genome (taxonomy, in-reference flag, NSTI, our nearest 16S identity, per-method KO F1/precision/recall/TP/FP/FN and module error).
  • ko_calls.tsv.gz (results only): genome × KO, truth, PICRUSt2 copy number and our probabilities.
  • module_calls.tsv.gz (results only): genome × module completeness, truth and every method.
  • per_ko.tsv: per KO, with name: prevalence, AUROC and F1 per method.
  • results/pilot/aim1/<arm>_<level>/predictions/*.parquet: all out-of-fold predictions of our models.
  • results/pilot/picrust2_out/: PICRUSt2's own outputs (KO copy numbers, NSTI, reference genome list).

Q4. Ordination of predicted against true profiles.

Predicted against true functional profiles in one ordination. Per row, the true profiles of the 1,205 unseen genomes (grey) and each method's predictions for the same genomes share one PCoA. Top: KO presence (Jaccard). Bottom: module completeness (Bray–Curtis). Thin lines join a genome's true and predicted profile.

Numbers in each panel: Mantel r (do predicted genome-to-genome distances follow the true ones; 1 = yes), Procrustes m² (shape mismatch; 0 = same), PERMANOVA R² (share of variation explained by predicted vs true; 0 = same centre), ANOSIM R (separation of the two clouds; 0 = none) and spread = PERMDISP (distance to centroid; below truth = predictions pulled towards typical profiles). 999 permutations swap labels within each genome (paired design).

Takeaway: all methods sit on top of the truth: PERMANOVA R² ≤ 0.02 for KOs and ≤ 0.06 for modules. With 1,205 paired genomes, every test reaches p = 0.001, so the effect sizes are what matter. 1-NN reproduces the landscape best (Mantel 0.94; R² 0.0003; spread 0.50 vs 0.50 in the truth). PICRUSt2 keeps the centre (R² 0.005) but scrambles which genomes are alike (Mantel 0.72). The random forest shrinks profiles most (module spread 0.16 vs 0.27; ANOSIM R 0.17).

random forest 0.82 0.0205 0.038 0.425

Q5. How the methods differ.

ours PICRUSt2 2.6.4 (default)
reference GTDB R232, CheckM2 ≥ 90 % / ≤ 5 %; pilot ~1,600 per fold, full ~44,000 PICRUSt2-SC: GTDB r214, 27,870 genomes
reference annotation eggNOG-mapper 2.1.15, DB 5.0.2 eggNOG-mapper 2.1.12, DB 5.0.2 (same pipeline as our truth)
16S processing SINA alignment (SILVA 144); positions as features HMMER + EPA-ng placement into a 16S tree
prediction k-NN on 16S identity; random forest / LightGBM on alleles hidden-state prediction on the tree (maximum parsimony)
output KO probability, module completeness, COG composition KO copy number; pathways via MinPath
amplicons one model per primer pair any fragment placed on the full-length tree
novelty measure 16S identity to nearest training genome NSTI; NSTI > 2 dropped
built-in validation clade-blocked CV, genus to class none; NSTI as a warning

Caveat. PICRUSt2 can be given a custom reference. Running it with our training folds as its reference would remove the reference-size difference and leave only the method difference. That is an option for the full run (§7).

6. What must change before full scale

  1. Aim 2 cannot run at 52k bacteria as built. Each phenotype runs pyseer separately. Each run re-reads an n × n kinship (≈ 30 GB as text at 52k) and re-decomposes it (O(n³)). Even with pyseer's --save-lmm / --load-lmm (decompose once), each phenotype costs O(n² × variants): about 1 CPU-h per phenotype at 52k, or ~4,600 CPU-h in total. Options: run Aim 2 on a stratified subsample (~15k bacteria: ~5 min per phenotype, ~12 h on 32 cores), plus --save-lmm.
  2. PICRUSt2 used 61.5 GB for 2k queries. Its placement step should run in chunks (sequences are independent), e.g. 2k per task. The comparison step (§5) should run on the same chunks.
  3. Patristic distances use a dense n × n matrix (D063). At 55k that is 12 GB, and the kinship it is built from is larger still. It needs a nearest-relative-on-tree computation instead of all pairs.

None of these touches the per-genome steps, which take most of the time.

7. Open decisions for the full run

  1. Scale. All 54,963 filtered genomes: ~7 days of eggNOG, ~260 GB of work disk. Or a stratified 20k subset: ~2.5 days. The case for 55k is that Aim 1 accuracy depends on reference density (fig 1). The full set is also the only way to test whether learned models beat k-NN when data is plentiful.
  2. Aim 2 sample (§6.1): stratified subsample of about 15k bacteria, or another size.
  3. Aim 2 homoplasy criterion (§4). Options: require ≥ 5 independent origins of the allele, or require the association to replicate within ≥ 2 independent orders (test within clades).
  4. PICRUSt2 with our reference. Optionally rerun PICRUSt2 with a custom reference built from our training folds, to compare methods on an equal reference (§5, caveat). Cost: one reference build and one placement per fold.
  5. Still open from the design: D048 (fixed hyperparameters, no inner CV), D060 (GC-enrichment control instead of a stem map), and D019 (Aim 2 bacteria only; the pilot has 204 archaea).
